summary:
Second Kings continues 1 Kings — the two were originally one book — and carries the divided kingdoms to their ends: Israel falls to Assyria in 722 BC, Judah to Babylon in 586. It opens as a chariot of fire with horses of fire separates Elijah from Elisha, "and Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind" (2:11). Elisha has asked for "a double portion of your spirit" (2:9) — the firstborn son's share of an inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17). His miracles follow: a widow's oil multiplied to pay her debt, the Shunammite woman's dead son raised, and Naaman, commander of the army of Aram, cured of leprosy after washing seven times in the Jordan (ch. 5) — the foreigner Jesus singles out in Luke 4:27.

In Israel, Jehu — anointed at Elisha's instruction — destroys Ahab's house: Jezebel is thrown from a window, fulfilling Elijah's word at Naboth's vineyard, and "Jehu eradicated Baal from Israel" (10:28); Hosea 1:4 later announces judgment on his dynasty for "the bloodshed of Jezreel." Coups follow until Samaria falls to Assyria after a three-year siege in 722 BC and the people are deported. The narrator stops to explain (17:7–23): "All this happened because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt" — worship at high places (local hilltop shrines outside the Jerusalem temple), sons and daughters sacrificed in fire, the prophets, God's messengers, ignored — until "Israel was exiled from their homeland into Assyria, where they are to this day."

Judah outlives the north by 136 years. When Sennacherib of Assyria invades in 701 BC (chs. 18–19), King Hezekiah spreads the Assyrian ultimatum before the LORD in the temple, and the prophet Isaiah promises the city will stand; that night "the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000" in the Assyrian camp (19:35). Sennacherib's own inscriptions boast of shutting Hezekiah in Jerusalem "like a caged bird" but never claim the city. Manasseh then reigns fifty-five years, filling Jerusalem with idols and innocent blood; the book traces Judah's final sentence to his sins (24:3–4). Under Josiah, temple repairs turn up a scroll, often identified with some form of Deuteronomy — "I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD!" (22:8) — and his reform of 622 BC purges the high places and keeps a Passover unmatched "from the days of the judges" (23:22). "Neither before nor after Josiah was there any king like him" (23:25); yet the prophetess Huldah has already given the verdict: disaster will come, though not in Josiah's lifetime (22:15–20).

The end comes quickly. Josiah is killed at Megiddo in 609 BC confronting Pharaoh Neco, and Babylon soon replaces Assyria as the region's master. Nebuchadnezzar takes Jerusalem in 597 BC, deporting King Jehoiachin with the temple treasures; when his uncle Zedekiah rebels, the Babylonians return, burn the temple and the city, and carry Judah into exile in 586 BC (ch. 25). But the final scene jumps thirty-seven years into the exile: a new Babylonian king frees Jehoiachin from prison, sets his throne "above the thrones of the other kings who were with him in Babylon," and the book's last sentence reads, "And the king provided Jehoiachin a daily portion for the rest of his life" (25:27–30). Many read the notice as deliberate — David's line, promised an enduring throne (2 Samuel 7:16), is still alive — and Matthew's genealogy runs through this Jehoiachin ("Jeconiah") from David to Jesus (Matthew 1:11–12).
